question: For this read-only workload, which interconnect finishes sooner at equal 16 KiB capacity: an 8x8 full crossbar with 8 banks (A) or a radix-4 butterfly with 16 banks (B)?

cases.title: Pattern M: the bank-only model picks the slower design

mechanism.hypothesis: Internal route contention: in BFLY4 8x16, initiators 2k and 2k+1 share stage-1 router k; two requests whose bank IDs share bits [3:2] compete for one router output even when their banks differ. The bank-only model charges only bank conflicts.

observations.statement: Measured acceptance windows for M: LIC 40, BFLY4 RTL 64, bank-only model 32; makespans 41 / 33 / 65.
Pattern L isolates it: eight distinct banks on both designs, yet the butterfly RTL needs 65 cycles while the model predicts 33.
Pattern B has no shared stage-1 outputs and the bank-only model is exact (33 = 33).

Measured inside the RTL (diagnostic trace, boundary events identical to the reference run): some stage-1 router output has two or more competing requests in M 59 of 65 cycles, L 59 of 65 cycles, B 0 of 33 cycles.
Adding exactly one shared link per (initiator pair, bank>>2) resolves 13 of 13 development witnesses and cuts held-out reversals 3 → 0 across both sealed baskets.

alternatives.why: Pattern B: model 33 vs RTL 33 cycles; every response passes the bank/row data check
Gate 0A single-read calibration fixes A_4 → V_5; adding a cycle of response latency gives 20 development reversals (parent 13)
unfair round robin leaves 7 of 13 development witnesses unresolved
fitted penalties leave 3 of 13 witnesses unresolved; independent verification: REJECTED (R1, R2, R4, R5)

cases.summary: Supplied calibration: initiators 0-6 repeat words 0-6; initiator 7 reads word 8 eight times, then word 7.
limitations: One stress workload; not a deployment-wide claim.

cases.title: Pattern L: the model cannot tell the designs apart
cases.summary: Initiator i repeatedly reads word i.

cases.title: Pattern B: model and hardware agree
cases.summary: Words [0,8,1,9,2,10,3,11]: crossbar bank conflicts, no butterfly route conflicts.
limitations: Agreement here does not validate the model elsewhere.

cases.title: Wrong bank mapping: a tie that costs almost double
cases.summary: The authored defect maps banks with q mod 8 on a 16-bank butterfly; the model ties and the tie policy picks the crossbar.
limitations: Not a strict reversal: the model's ordering is below the margin; tie-policy regret is in the details.

cases.title: Invalid reference: an injected monitor fault blocks the comparison
cases.summary: Pattern M with a deliberately injected payload-routing monitor fault on the design-B reference run.
limitations: Deliberate instrument control: the fault is injected into the monitor's view, not the design.

global_limitations: Cycles at a common abstract clock; no silicon speed, area, power or frequency claim.
RTL simulation is a reference implementation, not fabricated silicon.
Audit cases were authored by the implementer; none is independently authored or naturally occurring.

implemented: Pinned RTL and toolchain, verified against locks
Verilator harness with 14 counted monitors and an independent event checker
Harness validation: 21/21 checks, every monitor catches an injected fault
L/B/M measured; strict reversal on M
Python and compiled C++ fast models, cross-checked event-for-event
Six-case discovery screen with six deterministic search methods
Unrestricted formal proof of 10 transport properties on the 2x2 harness
Structural repair accepted on two sealed held-out baskets; three wrong repairs rejected
Measured internal router activity from diagnostic traces
Static, Cloudflare-ready viewer over executed artifacts
Decision map: 289 workloads on both RTL designs; the bank-only model picks the wrong design in 11 and cannot decide in 16 more; the repaired model: 2 and 14
not_done: Model speed: 1.7x end-to-end (5x target not met; simulation kernel alone 2-8x). Process start-up and workload I/O dominate; Verilator is already fast on this small design.
No independently authored or naturally occurring audit case
